title: The Honest Thief and the Pearl Necklace (ZH)
summary: A burglar breaks into a house to steal food for his starving sister, but refuses to take a diamond necklace. Birbal recognizes his noble spark.
full_text:
A young burglar named Shravan was caught inside the mansion of a wealthy imperial merchant. On the floor beside the burglar lay an open jewel box containing a diamond necklace worth ten thousand rupees, but in the burglar's sack, the guards found only two loaves of bread, a sack of rice, and a pot of milk.

Brought before Emperor Akbar, the merchant demanded: 'Sire! He is a burglar! Execute him!'

Birbal examined the evidence and asked the youth: 'Shravan, the diamond necklace was right in your hands. Why did you leave a ten-thousand-rupee treasure behind, and take only bread and rice?'

The young man wept with head bowed:

'My lord, my eight-year-old sister is dying of starvation in our mud hut. I have looked for honest work for three weeks, but finding none, I broke into this house to steal food to keep her alive tonight.

'When I opened the chest and saw the diamond necklace, I was tempted. But my late mother's voice echoed in my conscience: "Steal not what is vanity; take only what preserves life in extremity, and confess your sin before God!"

'I could not bring myself to steal jewels. I took only bread for my sister, intending to turn myself in to the city watch once she was fed.'

The merchant scoffed: 'Lies! A thief is a thief!'

Birbal sent guards to the youth's hut, and confirmed the story: the little girl was starving in rags, waiting for her brother.

Birbal turned to Emperor Akbar with deep emotion:

'Sire, this boy broke the law out of desperate love for his starving sister, yet even in his crime, his conscience refused to touch gold or diamonds!

'A boy who possesses such an instinctive spark of honor under the pressure of starvation is not a hardened criminal; he is an honest soul driven to the edge by despair.

'If we hang him, we murder a noble heart and leave an orphan to die. But if we nurture his honor, we gain a faithful servant of the crown!'

Akbar was moved to tears. He pardoned Shravan, granted his family a permanent food allowance, and appointed the youth to the palace guard, where Shravan served with unswerving loyalty for thirty years.

Akbar thanked Birbal for distinguishing between malice and desperate sorrow.
